sources.title: Halbjahresbericht 2025/2: Cyberbedrohungen in der Schweiz
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: 29,006 voluntary reports in H2 2025; fraud 52%; SMS blasters used in Switzerland from summer 2025.

sources.title: Internet Crime Report 2025
sources.evidence: Victims aged 60+: 201,266 complaints, about $7.7 billion in losses. Elder fraud (60+): 201,266 complaints, $7.748 billion losses; Tech/Customer Support reported by 60+: 21,333 complaints and $1,040,730,043 losses (pp. 45–46).

sources.title: Protecting Older Consumers 2025–2026
sources.evidence: Reported losses by people 60+ over $3 billion in 2025.

sources.title: Schockanruf durch falsche Polizisten
sources.evidence: Crying voice, in some cases AI-generated; hang up, call the person directly or 117; police never ask for money by phone.

sources.title: Angebliche Polizisten rufen wieder ältere Personen an
sources.evidence: Manipulated numbers, even the police number; call 117 after hanging up and waiting for the dial tone.

sources.title: Vorsicht bei Telefonanrufen mit Bandansagen
sources.evidence: Press 1 connects to fake officer; Swiss mobile numbers spoofed; goal remote-control program; police never play recordings.

sources.title: Telefonbetrug
sources.evidence: “Legen Sie einfach auf!”; fake police steps; shock call; remote support scam; fake bank security.

sources.title: Phishing, Vishing und Smishing
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: No bank asks by email to change passwords or verify card data; senders easily faked; report to antiphishing.ch.

sources.title: Finanzieller Schaden
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: Contact bank immediately to block; many have 24-hour block hotlines; report to police.

sources.title: Sicher twinten
sources.evidence: Staff never ask you to share passwords or access data; TWINT, its partners and your bank never ask for your security code; keep your PIN to yourself; enter it only in the TWINT app; scan TWINT QR codes only with the TWINT app, not the phone camera; don't pay with 5-digit codes someone sent you; payment links start with https://go.twint.ch/; send money only to people you know; check name, number and amount; be careful on marketplaces; if scammed call your bank immediately; forward suspicious mail to abuse@twint.ch.

sources.title: Report a cyber incident
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: Not processed around the clock; acute emergency: call 112 or 117.

sources.title: 112: the European emergency number
sources.evidence: Free, works everywhere in the EU.

sources.title: Find help or report abuse
sources.publisher: US Department of Justice, Elder Justice Initiative
sources.evidence: If this is an emergency, call 9-1-1.

sources.title: Scammers use fake emergencies to steal your money
sources.evidence: Voice cloning from a short clip; don’t trust the voice; hang up and call back on a known number.

sources.title: Criminals use generative AI to facilitate financial fraud (PSA)
sources.evidence: Create a secret word or phrase with your family.

sources.title: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
sources.evidence: Signs of phishing; contact the company on a number or website you know is real; forward to reportphishing@apwg.org.

sources.title: How to recognize and report spam text messages
sources.evidence: Fake package notices; companies won’t ask for account info by text; forward to 7726.

sources.title: Scammers hide harmful links in QR codes
sources.evidence: Don’t scan an unexpected QR code in an email or text.

sources.title: Caller ID spoofing
sources.evidence: Caller ID can be falsified; if a recording asks you to press a button, hang up.

sources.title: Cyber actors exploit “secure” websites in phishing campaigns (PSA)
sources.evidence: Do not trust a website just because it has a lock icon or https.

sources.title: Use strong passwords
sources.publisher: US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
sources.evidence: Long (16+), random, unique; passphrase of 4–7 words; use a password manager.

sources.title: Turn on multifactor authentication
sources.publisher: US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
sources.evidence: Turn on MFA, starting with email.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned
sources.evidence: Check if your email address is in a data breach.

sources.title: Make text easier to read on iPhone
sources.evidence: Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text.

sources.title: Report spam and block senders in Messages on iPhone
sources.evidence: Swipe left, Delete and Report Spam; Report Spam link for unknown senders.

sources.title: Screen and block calls on iPhone
sources.evidence: Settings > Apps > Phone: screen or silence unknown callers; block a contact.

sources.title: Use contacts from the Phone app on iPhone
sources.evidence: Add to Favorites.

sources.title: Add and use contact information on iPhone
sources.evidence: Contacts app, tap +, enter name and number, tap Done.

sources.title: Browse the web using Safari on iPhone
sources.evidence: Touch and hold a link to see a preview without opening the page.

sources.title: Bookmark a website in Safari on iPhone
sources.evidence: Add a bookmark.

sources.title: Use the Passwords app on your iPhone
sources.evidence: Passwords app from iOS 18; warns about weak, reused or leaked passwords.

sources.title: Use passwords on iPhone
sources.evidence: Security recommendations in the Passwords app.

sources.title: Find saved passwords and passkeys on your iPhone
sources.evidence: Open the Passwords app.

sources.title: Change text & display settings
sources.evidence: Settings > search Font size > slider.

sources.title: Report spam & block numbers in Google Messages
sources.evidence: Touch and hold the conversation > Block > Report spam > OK.

sources.title: See caller ID & spam protection
sources.evidence: More options > Settings > Caller ID and spam; Filter spam calls.

sources.title: Add, find & edit contacts on Android
sources.evidence: Contacts app > Add > name and number > Save.

sources.title: Manage passwords in Chrome (Android)
sources.evidence: Chrome offers to save; Google Password Manager; add a password.

sources.title: Manage passwords in Google Password Manager (Android)
sources.evidence: Save and manage passwords.

sources.title: Change compromised passwords in your Google Account (Password Checkup)
sources.evidence: Check if saved passwords are exposed, weak or reused; start Password Checkup.

sources.title: Make your account more secure
sources.evidence: Security Checkup; add a recovery phone and email.

sources.title: Create, find & edit bookmarks in Chrome (Android)
sources.evidence: More > Add to bookmarks.

sources.title: antiphishing.ch
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: Report phishing pages via web form; forward phishing emails to reports@antiphishing.ch; run by BACS.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned: Who, what and why
sources.evidence: Created and run by Troy Hunt since 2013 as a free resource.

sources.title: Turn on 2-Step Verification (Android)
sources.evidence: Open your Google Account > Security & sign-in > under 'How you sign in to Google' select Turn on 2-Step Verification > follow the on-screen steps; an extra layer of security in case your password is stolen.

sources.title: Two-factor authentication for Apple Account
sources.evidence: Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > turn on two-factor authentication; a six-digit verification code is displayed on trusted devices or sent to the trusted phone number; two-factor authentication is the default for most accounts.

sources.title: Passkeys
sources.evidence: FAQ: 'Passkeys are a password replacement technology … a passkey is a secret stored on one's devices, unlocked by the user the same way they unlock their device (biometrics, security key, PIN, pattern, etc.). Unlike passwords, passkeys are phishing-resistant, are always strong …'

sources.title: Sign in with a passkey instead of a password
sources.evidence: Sign in with fingerprint, face scan or screen lock PIN; passkeys can't be shared, copied, written down or accidentally given to someone else, so more secure against phishing; create: go to myaccount.google.com/signinoptions/passkeys > Create a passkey; only create passkeys on devices you personally own; anyone who can unlock your device can access the account; Android 9 / iOS 16 or later.

sources.title: Use passkeys to sign in to websites and apps on iPhone
sources.evidence: Passkeys are uniquely generated per account and less vulnerable to phishing; requires iCloud Keychain and two-factor authentication; when you see the option to save a passkey tap Continue; if no option the site doesn't support passkeys; sign in by tapping the account name field, the suggested name, then Face ID/Touch ID or device passcode; stored in the Passwords app.

sources.title: About the security of passkeys
sources.evidence: Passkeys are resistant to phishing, always strong, no shared secrets; public key stored on the server, private key never learned by the server.

sources.title: Sign in with backup codes (Android)
sources.evidence: Backup codes for when you lose your phone or can't get codes; each 8-digit code works once; a new set of 10 whenever you want, old set becomes inactive; do not share backup codes; Google never asks for a backup code other than at sign in; store somewhere safe like where you keep your passport; Settings > Google > Manage your Google Account > Security & sign-in > 2-Step Verification > Backup codes > Continue > Get backup codes.

sources.title: Set up a recovery contact for your Apple Account
sources.evidence: A recovery contact is someone you designate who can get a recovery code for you; they have no access to your account; Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Recovery Contacts > Add Recovery Contact; needs iOS 15 or later.

sources.title: S-U-P-E-R.ch – Carry out regular updates
sources.evidence: All software contains vulnerabilities; cybercriminals exploit them to take control of devices, infect them with malware and steal login or card data; activate the automatic update function for the operating system and all programmes and apps; use the latest browser version.

sources.title: Geräteschutz, Passwörter und Zugriffsschutz
sources.evidence: Make sure all devices install security updates automatically; outdated software is a gateway for criminals; only download software and apps from official manufacturer sites or official app stores; on mobile, download apps only from recognised stores and check ratings and permissions.

sources.title: Update Software
sources.evidence: Page marked as archived content. 'Many software updates are created to fix security risks'; turn on automatic updates in the device's or application's security settings.

sources.title: Update your iPhone or iPad
sources.evidence: Keeping software up to date is one of the most important things for security; Settings > General > Software Update > Automatic Updates > turn on Automatically Install (installs overnight while charging on Wi-Fi) / Automatically Download; back up, plug into power, use Wi-Fi.

sources.title: Check & update your Android version
sources.evidence: Connect to Wi-Fi, charge to at least 75%; most system updates and security patches install automatically; when notified, open the notification and tap the update action; or Settings > System > Software updates (Pixel); steps can vary by device.

sources.title: Install Windows Updates
sources.evidence: Windows 11/10: Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates > Download & install; restart if prompted.

sources.title: Update macOS on Mac
sources.evidence: Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update; Software Update automatically checks for new software; use Software Update settings to control whether your Mac downloads or installs updates automatically.

sources.title: Update apps or use automatic downloads on iPhone
sources.evidence: Apps downloaded from the App Store update automatically by default on iPhone and iPad; manual: App Store > My Account / your photo > App Updates.

sources.title: How to update apps on Android
sources.evidence: Updating apps improves app security; Google Play > profile picture > Settings > Network Preferences > Auto-update apps > choose an option.

sources.title: How to spot, avoid, and report tech support scams
sources.evidence: Fake pop-up warnings urge you to call a number; scammers ask for remote access, pretend to find a virus and charge a fee; they want gift cards, wire, crypto or payment apps; legitimate tech companies won't contact you to say there's a problem with your computer; real security pop-ups never ask you to call a phone number; talk to someone you trust; report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. (Fetched via WebFetch; direct fetch returns 404 to scripts.)

sources.title: Protect yourself from tech support scams
sources.evidence: Microsoft doesn't make unsolicited calls or send unsolicited email to provide tech support; Microsoft error and warning messages never include phone numbers; scammers may put the browser in full screen with pop-ups that won't go away; with remote access they install malware; download software only from official sites or the Microsoft Store.

sources.title: Falsche Sicherheitswarnung beim Surfen im Internet
sources.evidence: Fake security warning with a number; caller poses as Microsoft or Apple support, has victim install remote maintenance software, then leads to payment page or e-banking; do not call; Windows: Ctrl+Alt+Del, Task Manager, end the browser; Mac: Cmd+Option+Esc, Force Quit the browser; if you gave access: call bank, change passwords, have the computer reset, report to cantonal police.

sources.title: Woche 41: Entwicklung bei Fake Support
sources.evidence: Fake support: callers pose as IT firm such as Microsoft; browser lock pages with often Swiss phone numbers, sometimes a voice; neither browser nor computer is really locked; closing the browser or restarting helps; never call the number; never allow remote access; if you did, have a specialist check the computer.

sources.title: Woche 15: Falsche Bankmitarbeiter fordern Installation von Fernwartungssoftware
sources.evidence: 14 April 2026: rise in calls from fake bank staff (also BAKOM) who connect to an 'IT specialist' and push installation of AnyDesk, TeamViewer etc.; with access they see the screen, control the mouse, steal passwords and access e-banking; banks, card companies and authorities never ask by phone to install remote software; end such calls; uninstall and change passwords if installed; report to local police if money lost.

sources.title: Use Google Play Protect
sources.evidence: Play Protect runs a safety check on apps from Google Play before download, checks device for harmful apps from other sources, warns and may remove them; on by default; recommended to always keep on; Play Store > profile icon > Play Protect > Settings.

sources.title: App Store
sources.evidence: 'We conduct a thorough review to check that apps come from known sources, are free of known malware …'; App product pages show rankings and reviews.
